questions.stem: An 18-year-old woman presented with new onset lowgrade fever, sore throat, and painful joints. She had just recovered from a 2-week bout of diarrhea which she ascribed to eating some undercooked pork. She did not take regular medications and had no recent travel outside of the United States. On exam, her throat was unremarkable. Her small and large joints were normal. Multiple tender nodules 3–4 cm in diameter were palpable over both shins. Her serum TSH was noted to be elevated although she showed no signs of Graves’ disease.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Yersinia enterocolitica Erythema nodosum and reactive arthritis can be seen following infection with Yersinia enterocolitica which can be acquired through consumption of undercooked meat, especially pork products. Postinfectious immunologic sequelae (e.g., reactive arthritis and erythema nodosum) can develop 2 weeks after the diarrheal illness. Twenty percent of patients may present with pharyngitis, which is not seen in other causes of gastroenteritis. Throat cultures may also yield positive growth for Y. enterocolitica. Although Yersinia does not cause thyroiditis, it shares antigens that resemble TSH and hence cross-react with antibodies in Graves’ disease.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q18

questions.question: 12.  Terminal ileitis in a patient on an iron chelator.

parts.text: B.  Give three alternate bacterial diagnoses.

cohort_answer.text:
Yersinia enterolitica terminal ileitis
Salmonella, MTB,MAI, Yersinia pseudotuberculosis
3rd gen cephalosporin, mero, cipro,tazo, doxy, gent, septra (r- 1st/2nd gen cephalosporins, macrolides, vanco)

questions.question: Terminal ileitis in a patient on an iron chelator

parts.text: B) Give 3 alternate bacterial diagnoses? Alternate question: give 1 viral cause

cohort_answer.text:
Yersinia enterocolitica
Best 3 answers: Salmonella enterica subspp enteritidis; C. diff; TB. Probably: V. vulnificus (also siderophilic); L. monocytogenes (also siderophilic); Actinomycosis. Viral: CMV
For yersinia colitis treatment only if severe with doxycycline or ciprofloxacin (Sanford). If bacteremia or sepsis with yersinia causing bacteremia ceftriaxone, or ciprofloxacin (TMPSMX an alternative option)
